txhome

txhome helps you explore how Texas housing markets weathered the 2008 financial crisis. It contains monthly housing data for 46 Texas market areas from 2000 to 2015, a function that measures how far each market fell during the crisis and how quickly it recovered, and an interactive Shiny app for comparing markets.

Website: https://etc5523-2026.github.io/etc5523-assignment-4-chenulidias/

Who it’s for and the question it answers

The package is designed for economics students studying how the 2008 financial crisis affected regional housing markets. It helps answer:

Which Texas housing markets were hit hardest by the 2007-2010 downturn, and how quickly did they recover?

The 2007-2009 financial crisis was the worst US downturn since the Great Depression, and it is widely studied in economics because it began in the housing market. Texas is a well-known case: it escaped the worst of the crash, but its local markets were not affected equally (Kumar and Skelton, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, 2013).

The package lets students compare how far different Texas markets fell and how quickly they recovered, and see why economists adjust prices for inflation: in this data, many markets only appear unaffected until inflation is removed. The data is ready to use, the app needs no coding and explains each measure in plain language, and crisis_recovery() gives the figures for any market in one line.

Installation

Install the package from GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-chenulidias")

The package requires R 4.1 or later. Its dependencies (dplyr, shiny, bslib, ggplot2 and scales) are installed automatically.

Launch the app 

library(txhome)
run_app()

In the app, choose one or more market areas and a measure (homes sold, or the median sale price with or without an adjustment for inflation). Two headline boxes show which chosen area was hit hardest and which recovered fastest, and three tabs show the areas over time, a summary table, and a ranking of every area in Texas.

Use the summary function

crisis_recovery() summarises each area’s pre-crisis peak, downturn low, percentage fall and recovery year:

crisis_recovery(measure = "sales", areas = c("Austin", "Dallas", "Houston"))

For example, home sales in Austin, Dallas and Houston each fell by roughly 30-35% from 2006 to 2010. Austin was back at its pre-crisis level by 2013, while Dallas had still not recovered by mid-2015.

Data

The package includes one dataset, tx_housing_markets: monthly sales, prices, listings and inventory for 46 Texas market areas from January 2000 to July 2015.

  • Housing data: collected by the Texas A&M University (TAMU) Real Estate Center (https://trerc.tamu.edu/), using the copy distributed in the ggplot2 package as ggplot2::txhousing.
  • Inflation data: the Consumer Price Index for the US South region (CUUR0300SA0) from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, retrieved from FRED (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CUUR0300SA0). It is used to convert median prices into July 2015 dollars, so prices from different years can be compared fairly.

The script data-raw/tx_housing_markets.R prepares the data: it renames city to area (since many are counties or regions), converts decimal years into proper monthly dates, labels each month as pre-crisis (2000-2006), downturn (2007-2010) or recovery (2011-2015), and joins the inflation data to calculate inflation-adjusted median prices. To recreate the dataset, run source("data-raw/tx_housing_markets.R") from the package’s source folder. See ?tx_housing_markets for a description of every column.

Limitations: the data end in July 2015, so later recoveries are not captured; market areas are MLS (multiple listing service) regions rather than exact city boundaries; and two areas (Kerrville and South Padre Island) have no data before 2007, so their fall and recovery cannot be measured.
